title-group.article-title: High-density lipoprotein mediates silica nanoparticle recognition by the multiligand receptor SR-B1

abstract.p: Scavenger receptor class B type 1 (SR-B1), best known as a high-density lipoprotein (HDL) receptor, is now recognized as a multi-ligand membrane receptor. In addition to HDL, SR-B1 binds low-density lipoprotein (LDL), hepatitis C virus, Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and inorganic silica particles. However, the mechanisms by which SR-B1 recognizes diverse ligands remain unclear. We previously reported that a basic amino acid cluster consisting of K151, K156, and K395 at the extracellular apex of SR-B1 is essential for charge-dependent binding to silica and is distinct from the known HDL-binding site. In this study, homology modeling of SR-B1 revealed the HDL-binding site is oriented toward the basic cluster. Site-directed mutagenesis demonstrated that this basic cluster is required for HDL and, to a lesser extent, LDL binding, which in turn promotes binding to silica nanoparticles. The selective binding of SR-B1 to silica nanoparticles, but not to titanium dioxide nanoparticles, latex nanoparticles, monosodium urate crystals, or multiwalled carbon nanotubes, depends on specific HDL–silica or LDL–silica interactions. These findings suggest that HDL, and potentially LDL, may underlie SR-B1's function as a mutiligand membrane receptor.

body.p: The scavenger receptor class B type 1 (SR-B1 or SR-BI, also called CLA-1), encoded by Scarb1 gene (1), is a well-established high-density lipoprotein (HDL) receptor (2, 3, 4). SR-B1 plays an essential role in lipid metabolism by binding HDL and selectively transferring cholesteryl esters into cells (5, 6). In addition to HDL, SR-B1 binds low-density lipoprotein (LDL) (7, 8), and anionic phospholipids (9, 10), the latter property of which may enable recognition of diverse pathogens containing these lipids (4, 6). For example, hepatitis C virus (HCV) (11, 12, 13) exploits SR-B1 for entry, and SR-B1 also binds Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (14, 15). Thus, SR-B1 is thought to play important roles in infectious disease (5, 6).

Beyond biological ligands, we and others have reported that SR-B1 binds inorganic silica (SiO2) particles (16, 17, 18). Because class A scavenger receptor such as scavenger receptor class A type 1 (SR-A1) was also known to bind silica (19, 20), both class A and class B receptors may be involved in toxicity of silica nanoparticles (21, 22) as well as silicosis, a chronic occupational lung disease (16, 23). Since these bioparticles and inorganic particles exhibit a negative surface charge at physiological pH (24, 25, 26), SR-B1 recognition is thought to rely not only on stereospecific interactions but also, and perhaps more importantly, on electrostatic interactions.

Structurally, SR-B1 contains two transmembrane domains at N and C termini, forming a large ectodomain loop, a common feature of other class B scavenger receptors LIMP-2 and CD36, which share ∼30% amino acid identify with SR-B1 (4, 6). Although the structure of SR-B1 has not been crystallized, homology modeling based on the crystal structure of LIMP-2 suggested that the apex α-helix serves as a putative ligand-binding site (27). Indeed, substitution of methionine 159 in the α-helix with glutamic acid abolishes binding to both HDL (27) and LDL (8). In contrast, our previous work identified a basic amino acid cluster (K151, K156, K395) at the extracellular apex as essential for charge-dependent silica binding (16). These findings suggested distinct modes of interaction between SR-B1 and HDL versus silica (16).

However, critical gaps remain in our understanding of how SR-B1 recognizes diverse ligands. Although M159 has been implicated in HDL binding and the basic cluster in silica binding, it remains unknown whether M159 also contributes to silica recognition and, conversely, whether the basic cluster is required for HDL binding. Moreover, the mechanism by which SR-B1 selectively binds silica but not other negatively charged inorganic particles, such as titanium dioxide (TiO2), latex, or monosodium urate (MSU) crystals (16), is not understood. We address these questions here to explain how SR-B1 functions as a multiligand receptor, capable of recognizing both biological and inorganic ligands.

sec.title: M159A, but not M159E, mutant of SR-B1 binds silica, HDL, and LDL
sec.p:
We previously reported that an extracellular basic cluster of lysine residues at positions 151, 156, and 395 is essential for silica binding (16). In contrast, methionine 159, a hydrophobic residue, has been shown to be critical for the initial attachment to HDL (27, 28). However, whether the converse holds remained unknown. To address this, we first analyzed the spatial relationship between these residues. Based on homology modeling of mouse (m) SR-B1, M159 faces the basic cluster consisting of K151, K156, and K395 (Fig. 1A). To test whether M159 contributes to silica binding, we substituted this residue with alanine. WT mSR-B1 and the M159A mutant were fused at the C terminus to eGFP and expressed in HEK293T cells. Silica binding assays were performed in complete medium containing 10% fetal calf serum (FCS). Both WT SR-B1 and M159A efficiently associated with rhodamine-labeled silica nanoparticles (Fig. 1B), initially suggesting that SR-B1 associates with silica independently of HDL. However, we noticed that in previous studies, M159 was substituted with glutamic acid to demonstrate that this residue is essential for HDL and LDL binding (8, 27). We therefore additionally generated the M159E mutant and found that it completely lost the ability to associate with silica nanoparticles (Fig. 1B).Figure 1
M159A, but not M159E, mutant of SR-B1 associates with silica, HDL, and LDL.A, homology model of mouse (m) SR-B1. The dashed-boxed regions are enlarged on the right. The rightmost panel highlights side chains of M159 (yellow), K151, K156, and K395 (blue). B and C, HEK293T cells transiently expressing WT or mutant mSR-B1-eGFP were incubated for 30 min at 37 °C with rhodamine-labeled silica nanoparticles (10 μg/ml) in complete medium containing 10% FCS (B) or with DiI-labeled HDL (1 μg/ml) or DiI-labeled LDL (3 μg/ml) in FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% BSA (C). Rhodamine-silica nanoparticle or DiI-lipoprotein binding to eGFP-negative and eGFP-positive cells was analyzed by flow cytometry. Numbers in dot plots indicate the percentage of cells in each gate. In GFP-negative and GFP-positive populations, Δ median fluorescence intensity (ΔMFI) was calculated by subtracting the MFI of untreated cells from that of rhodamine-silica nanoparticle– or DiI-lipoprotein–treated cells. Data are shown as mean ± SD (n = 3). ns, not significant; ∗p < 0.05; ∗∗p < 0.01; two-way ANOVA. DiI, 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate; FCS, fetal calf serum; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-B1, scavenger receptor class B type 1.

We next conducted HDL- and LDL-association assays using lipoproteins labeled with 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate (DiI). Because FCS contains a substantial level of HDL and LDL, we used FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) to maintain cell viability. SR-B1 associated with DiI-HDL and, to a lesser extent, DiI-LDL (Fig. 1C). Consistent with prior reports (8, 27), M159E completely lost both fluorescence signals, whereas M159A unexpectedly retained both (Fig. 1C).

Given that SR-B1 reportedly mediates the uptake of DiI from HDL (2), we next performed confocal microscopy to determine whether SR-B1 internalizes silica and DiI or instead binds these ligands at the plasma membrane, and to identify which of these functions is lost in the M159E mutant. Consistent with the fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis, cells expressing WT-eGFP or M159A-eGFP, but not M159E-eGFP, preferentially associated with rhodamine-silica (Fig. 2A), DiI-HDL (Fig. 2B), and DiI-LDL (Fig. 2C), predominantly at the plasma membrane. Under our experimental conditions, neither rhodamine nor DiI appeared to be diffusely distributed within cells. Of course, we cannot rule out the possibility that the hydrophobic DiI is selectively taken up from HDL and incorporated into the plasma membrane. Taken together, these observations suggest that SR-B1 and M159A bind silica, HDL, and LDL, whereas M159E loses this binding activity. Taken together with the FACS analysis, these results suggest that M159 is dispensable for the initial interaction with HDL and LDL; rather, substitution with acidic glutamic acid likely neutralizes the nearby basic cluster, thereby abolishing binding to HDL, LDL, and silica.Figure 2
WT SR-B1 and M159A, but not M195E, mutant bind silica, HDL, and LDL. Indicated HEK293T cells were cultured with rhodamine-silica nanoparticles (A), DiI-HDL (B), or DiI-LDL (C), as in Figure 1. Then cells were analyzed by confocal microscopy. White bars indicate 10 μm. DiI, 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate; FCS, fetal calf serum; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-B1, scavenger receptor class B type 1.

sec.title: HDL binds the basic cluster and promotes silica binding
sec.p:
We next tested whether the basic cluster is required for HDL and LDL binding. Consistent with the HEK293T studies (Figs. 1 and 2), ectopic expression of mSR-B1 on BW5147 cells enabled these cells to associate with DiI-HDL at 37 °C (Fig. S1A). Compared with the 4 °C condition, the level of association was much higher at 37 °C, although the association was still predominantly at the plasma membrane (Figs. 3A and S1B), indicating the FACS signals primarily reflect surface binding and/or subsequent DiI incorporation into the plasma membrane. This binding was completely blocked by AOB-1, an anti-mouse SR-B1 mAb previously shown to inhibit silica binding (16) (Figs. 3B and S2). Consistent with our previous report (16), the KKK151/156/395AAA mutant lost the ability to bind silica nanoparticles, and we observed a similar loss of DiI-HDL binding (Figs. 3B and S2). Parallel findings were obtained in the DiI-LDL binding assay (Fig. 3, C and D). Taken together, these results indicate that this basic cluster is essential for binding not only to silica but also to HDL and LDL.Figure 3
HDL and LDL bind to the basic cluster of SR-B1.A and C, parental BW5147 cells and cells stably expressing mSR-B1 were incubated with 1 μg/ml DiI-HDL (A) or 3 μg/ml DiI-LDL (C) for 30 min at 37 °C in FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% BSA. Cells were then stained with AF488-phalloidin and analyzed by confocal microscopy. White bars indicate 10 μm. B and D, parental BW5147 cells and cells stably expressing mSR-B1 or the KKK151/156/395AAA mutant were left untreated or treated with 10 μg/ml of isotype control rat IgG2a (cIg) or AOB-1, an anti-mouse SR-B1 mAb, for 15 min. Cells were then incubated with or without 1 μg/ml DiI-HDL (B) or 3 μg/ml DiI-LDL (D) for 30 min at 37 °C in FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% BSA. DiI-lipoprotein binding was analyzed by flow cytometry. Red and black numbers in histograms indicate the MFI of DiI-lipoprotein–treated and DiI-lipoprotein–untreated cells, respectively. ΔMFI was calculated as in Figure 1C. Data are shown as mean ± SD (n = 3). ∗∗p < 0.01, one-way ANOVA. Similar results were obtained using a different lot of DiI-HDL and a different cell line (Fig. S2). DiI, 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate; FCS, fetal calf serum; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-B1, scavenger receptor class B type 1; BSA, bovine serum albumin; ΔMFI, Δ median fluorescence intensity.

To examine the effects of HDL and LDL in FCS on SR-B1 binding to silica, we depleted lipoproteins from FCS by KBr density gradient ultracentrifugation. Under these conditions, mSR-B1-eGFP–expressing HEK293T cells lost silica-binding activity (Fig. S3). Consistent with this finding, human (h) SR-B1 binding to silica (Fig. 4A) was abolished in FCS-free medium and was restored by the addition of purified HDL or LDL (Figs. 4B and S4). In contrast, lipid-free apoA-I, the major protein component of HDL, failed to restore binding (Fig. 4C), consistent with previous reports that lipid-free apoA-I has a much lower affinity for SR-B1 than HDL (29, 30). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that HDL and LDL, but not lipid-free apoA-I, bind the SR-B1 basic cluster, and promote its binding to silica.Figure 4
HDL and LDL promote SR-B1 binding to silica.A, parental Jurkat.EcoR cells and cells stably expressing human (h) SR-B1 were incubated with 3 μg/ml FITC-silica nanoparticles for 30 min at 37 °C. Cells were then stained with AF594-phalloidin and analyzed by confocal microscopy. White bars indicate 10 μm. B and C, Jurkat.EcoR cells expressing hSR-B1 were incubated with 3 μg/ml FITC-silica nanoparticles for 30 min at 37 °C in the presence or absence of 10 μg/ml (B) or the indicated concentrations (C) of unlabeled HDL, LDL, or apoA-I, either in complete medium containing 10% FCS or in FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% BSA. FITC-silica nanoparticle binding was analyzed by flow cytometry. Green and black numbers in histograms indicate MFI of FITC-silica–treated and –untreated cells, respectively (B). ΔMFI was calculated as described in Figure 1B. Data are shown as mean (green circles, triangles, and squares indicate HDL, LDL, and apoA-I, respectively) ± SD (n = 3). C, similar results were obtained using a different lot of HDL (Fig. S4). DiI, 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate; FCS, fetal calf serum; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-B1, scavenger receptor class B type 1; ΔMFI, Δ median fluorescence intensity; BSA, bovine serum albumin.

sec.title: HDL and LDL bind silica, but not other inorganic particles
sec.p:
We previously showed that SR-B1 binds silica but not TiO2, latex, MSU, or multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) in medium containing 10% FCS (16, 31). At the time, we interpreted this observation as direct binding of SR-B1 to silica; however, the mechanism underlying its inability to bind other particles remained unclear. The finding that HDL and LDL promote SR-B1–silica interactions prompted us to examine whether these lipoproteins bind different inorganic particles. As shown in Figure 5, DiI-HDL, and, to a lesser extent, DiI-LDL preferentially bound silica nanoparticles in a concentration-dependent manner, with minimal binding to TiO2, latex nanoparticles, MSU, or MWCNTs, even at the highest concentration tested. These results suggest that SR-B1 recognition of silica is promoted by the specific binding of HDL or LDL to silica.Figure 5
Specific binding of HDL and LDL to silica. Silica, TiO2, latex nanoparticles, monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, and multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) were incubated with the indicated concentrations of DiI-HDL (left panel) or DiI-LDL (right panel) for 30 min at 37 °C in FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% BSA. DiI-lipoprotein binding to particles was analyzed by flow cytometry. ΔMFI was calculated as described in Figure 1C. Data are shown as mean ± SD (n = 3). DiI, 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate; FCS, fetal calf serum; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-B1, scavenger receptor class B type 1; TiO2, titanium dioxide; ΔMFI, Δ median fluorescence intensity; BSA, bovine serum albumin.

sec.title: HDL and LDL do not contribute to silica binding to class A scavenger receptor SR-A1
sec.p:
Because silica also binds to the class A scavenger receptors in FCS-containing medium (16, 19, 20), we examined whether HDL and LDL contribute to SR-A1 binding to silica. In contrast to mSR-B1–expressing BW5147 cells, mSR-A1–expressing BW5147 cells did not bind HDL or LDL (Fig. 6A), consistent with a previous finding in hSR-A1–expressing HEK293 cells (32). To exclude the possibility that modified (oxidized or acetylated) LDL, known SR-A1 ligands (33), were present in FCS and contributed to this interaction, we repeated the assay in FCS-free medium; silica binding to SR-A1 was not abolished (Fig. 6B). Moreover, reconstitution with HDL or LDL did not enhance silica binding to SR-A1 (Fig. 6B). These results suggest that SR-A1 binds silica directly. Taken together, these findings support a model in which HDL or LDL binds the basic cluster of SR-B1 and promotes silica binding, whereas lipoproteins do not contribute to SR-A1 binding to silica (Fig. 7).Figure 6
HDL and LDL are not involved in SR-A1 binding to silica.A, parental BW5147 cells and cells stably expressing mSR-A1 were cultured with or without DiI-HDL (1 μg/ml) or DiI-LDL (3 μg/ml) and analyzed as in Figure 3B. B, FITC-silica nanoparticle (3 μg/ml) binding to parental BW5147 cells and cells stably expressing mSR-A1 in the presence or absence of unlabeled HDL or LDL (10 μg/ml each) was analyzed as in Figure 4B. DiI, 1,1‘-dioctadecyl-3,3,3‘3‘-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-A1, scavenger receptor class A type 1.Figure 7
Working model. HDL and LDL bind to the basic cluster (K151, K156, K395) of SR-B1, thereby promoting silica binding, whereas these lipoproteins do not mediate SR-A1 binding to silica. HDL, high-density lipoprotein; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; SR-A1, scavenger receptor class A type 1. Figure was drawn with BioRender.com.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we identified a basic cluster consisting of K151, K156, and K395 in the extracellular α-helix of SR-B1 as essential for HDL and LDL binding. In contrast, M159, previously reported as critical for the initial interaction with HDL and LDL (27, 28), was not required for lipoprotein binding. Instead, M159 may contribute indirectly by stabilizing the interaction between the basic cluster and HDL or LDL. Together, these findings establish the basic cluster as a key determinant of HDL and LDL recognition and highlight a potential novel target for therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating HDL–SR-B1 or LDL–SR-B1 interactions.

HDL and LDL are major circulating lipoproteins that are present at substantial levels in both human and mouse plasma (34). Intact HDL and LDL particles have not, to our knowledge, been detected in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, although apoA-I, a major protein component of HDL, has been reported in human bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (35, 36). However, when epithelial and endothelial barriers are compromised by silica-induced lung injury, plasma-derived lipoproteins are likely to gain access to the alveolar space and adsorb onto silica particles. Such lipoprotein-coated silica particles could be recognized by SR-B1–expressing lung macrophages, suggesting that plasma lipoproteins, such as HDL and LDL, may contribute to the toxicity of silica nanoparticles and the pathogenesis of silicosis (23).

Besides lipid metabolism, HDL has been implicated in several pathological processes. For example, HDL enhances HCV attachment to SR-B1 (37, 38), which functions as a coreceptor with CD81 for viral entry (13). HCV envelope proteins contain apolipoprotein E, and HCV particles are thought to associate with HDL (39). More recently, the HDL–SR-B1 axis was reported to facilitate severe acute respiratory sundrome cononravirus 2 entry via angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (40, 41). These observations underscore the broader role of HDL–SR-B1 interactions in pathological particle recognition.

Nanotechnology studies have demonstrated that proteins in biological fluids adsorb onto the surfaces of nanoparticles, forming a so-called “protein corona” (42, 43, 44). The corona profoundly influences nanoparticle toxicity and therapeutic efficacy (42, 43, 44). Silica nanoparticles, in particular, adsorb diverse serum proteins, including apolipoproteins (45, 46). Here we found that HDL binds strongly to silica but not to TiO2, latex nanoparticles, MSU, or MWCNTs. This specificity may reflect the abundance of positively charged residues in HDL apolipoproteins, which interact with negatively charged, hydrogen bond-rich silanol (Si-OH) groups of silica particles. These interactions provide a molecular explanation for why SR-B1 selectively binds silica, but not other inorganic particles (16).

In conclusion, our in vitro reconstitution assays, together with homology modeling, reveal that the apex basic cluster of SR-B1 is essential for the initial attachment to HDL, which in turn mediates silica particle binding. These findings suggest that this cluster is responsible not only for physiological HDL functions, such as lipid metabolism, but also for pathological functions, including the binding of silica particles or viral components. The generation of basic cluster–specific knock-in mutant mice will be useful for elucidating the in vivo physiological and pathological roles of this region.

sec.title: SR-B1 modeling
sec.p: Homology modeling of mSR-B1 was conducted using a crystallographic structure of human LIMP-2 protein (PDB: 4F7B chain A) previously (16). The model was analyzed by PyMOL Molecular Graphics System version 2.4.1 (http://www.pymol.org/).

sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: HEK293T cells (a human embryonic kidney–derived cell line; American Type Culture Collection) were maintained in complete Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium supplemented with 10% FCS, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, 2 mM glutamine, and 1 mM sodium pyruvate). Jurkat.EcoR cells (a human T-cell leukemia line, Jurkat cells transduced with the ecotropic receptor Slc7a) and BW5147 cells (a murine T-cell lymphoma line) stably expressing mSR-B1, hSR-B1, or mSR-A1 were generated previously (16) and maintained in complete RPMI. Mutant forms of mSR-B1 were generated by PCR-based mutagenesis using a vector harboring the mSR-B1 coding sequence as a template. WT and mutant forms of mSR-B1 were subcloned into pEGFP-N1 (Clontech) to fuse eGFP at the C terminus of mSR-B1. After confirmation of nucleotide sequences, these expression vectors were transiently transduced into HEK293T cells using PEI MAX (Mr 40,000; Polysciences).

sec.title: Particles
sec.p: Rhodamine-labeled amorphous silica nanoparticles (sicastar-redF, cat. #40-00-102; primary diameter 100 nm), FITC-labeled silica nanoparticles (sicastar-greenF, cat. #42-00-301; primary diameter 30 nm; cat. #42-00-102; primary diameter 100 nm), and FITC-labeled latex nanoparticles [latex-greenF, cat. #29-00-251, polymethacrylate (glycidyl methacrylate: methyl methacrylate: methacrylic acid = 80:10:10) copolymer particles (primary diameter 25 nm)] were purchased from micromod Partikeltechnologie GmbH. Nano-TiO2 crystals (cat. #637254; anatase:rutile, 80:20; primary diameter 21 nm) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. MSU crystals were prepared as described previously (16). In brief, 25 mM uric acid (Sigma-Aldrich) and 25 mM NaOH were dissolved in distilled water with stirring and boiling, and the solution was slowly cooled to 45 °C. After sterilization by filtration, the solution was stored at 4 °C for at least 5 days to allow precipitation of MSU crystals. MWCNTs (cat. #659258) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. DiI-human HDL was obtained from Alfa Aesar (Ward Hill, cat. #J65503, lot #9150315) and KALEN Biomedical, LLC (Montgomery Village, MD cat #770330-9, lot #42517501). DiI-human LDL (cat. #L3482, lot #3011684) was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Unlabeled human HDL was purchased from Alfa Aesar (cat. #J64903, lot #914C15A) and EMD Millipore Inc. (cat. #LP3-5 mg, lot #4291340), and unlabeled LDL (cat. #L3486, lot #3243141) was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific.

sec.title: Particle binding to cells
sec.p: HEK293T cells (2 × 105/well) were seeded in 24-well plates and cultured overnight. Jurkat.EcoR cells or BW5147 cells (2 × 105 each) were cultured in microtubes. Cells were incubated with the indicated concentrations of particles for 30 min at 37 °C. After incubation, cells were washed twice with PBS and harvested. Particle binding was analyzed using an Accuri C6 cytometer (BD Biosciences) or Symphony A1 flow cytometer (BD Biosciences), as described previously (31). For lipoprotein-depleted conditions, HDL- and LDL-free FCS was prepared by KBr density ultracentrifugation as described (47) with minor modifications. Briefly, FCS was adjusted to a density of 1.21 g/ml with KBr and centrifuged at 435,000g for 16 h at 4 °C. The bottom fraction was collected and dialyzed extensively with PBS. Cells were cultured in medium supplemented with 10% lipoprotein-depleted FCS. For FCS-free conditions, cells were cultured in medium containing 0.5% BSA (cat. #A7284, Sigma-Aldrich) to maintain cell viability, with or without the indicated concentrations of human HDL, LDL, or recombinant human apoA-I (cat. #019-20731, Fujifilm Wako Chemicals), and were analyzed as described above. For microscopy, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (cat. #163-20145, Fujifilm Wako Chemicals). In some assays, cells were then permeabilized with 0.05% Triton X-100 and stained with AF488-phalloidin (cat. #A12379, Invitrogen) or AF594-phalloidin (cat. #A12381, Invitrogen). Cells were analyzed using an LSM900 confocal laser-scanning microscope with Airyscan (Carl Zeiss AG).

sec.title: HDL and LDL binding to particles
sec.p: FITC-silica, TiO2, FITC-latex nanoparticles, MWCNTs (8.3 μg/100 μl each), as well as MSU (50 μg/100 μl each), were incubated with the indicated concentrations of DiI-HDL or DiI-LDL for 30 min at 37 °C in FCS-free medium supplemented with 0.5% BSA. After washing with PBS, particles were analyzed using a Symphony A1 flow cytometer (BD Biosciences). FITC-labeled particles were gated by fluorescence signal, whereas unlabeled particles were gated by side scatter signals, as described previously (16, 48). DiI-HDL and DiI-LDL binding to particles were then analyzed.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using one-way or two-way ANOVA, in GraphPad Prism version 10.1.1 (GraphPad Software): ∗<0.05 and ∗∗<0.01.
